title: Brønsted–Lowry acids and bases; Strong and weak acids
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AP Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: AB03#t3 term and clue written for the game; AB01#t1 term and clue written for the game; AB03#t1 term and clue written for the game; AB01#t2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: AB01#N.6b, AB03#N.3b, AB01#N.10, AB03#N.4b, AB01#N.11, AB03#N.7, AB03#N.11.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Concentration
items.clue: The amount of a dissolved substance per unit volume.

items.label: Brønsted–Lowry acid
items.clue: A species that donates a proton (H⁺) to another species.

items.label: Strong acid
items.clue: Dissociates effectively completely in water, as HNO₃ does.

items.label: Alkali
items.clue: A proton acceptor that dissolves in water, releasing OH⁻(aq).

questions.stem: The reaction HSO₄⁻(aq) + NH₃(aq) → SO₄²⁻(aq) + NH₄⁺(aq) occurs when the two species are mixed. Which choice gives the Brønsted–Lowry acid in the forward reaction, followed by its conjugate base?

options.text: HSO₄⁻, NH₃
HSO₄⁻, NH₄⁺
HSO₄⁻, SO₄²⁻
NH₃, NH₄⁺

questions.explanation: HSO₄⁻ gives a proton to NH₃, so it is the acid; what is left, SO₄²⁻, has one H fewer and one more negative charge: its conjugate base.

questions.stem: Two beakers at 25°C each contain 50 mL of an acid solution: one contains 0.10 M HCl(aq), and the other contains 0.10 M HA(aq), where HA is a weak monoprotic acid. Identical pieces of magnesium ribbon are dropped into the two beakers at the same moment. Which prediction about the first minute of the experiment is correct?

options.text: H₂ bubbles form at equal rates, because the two acid concentrations are equal
H₂ bubbles form faster in the HCl beaker, because its [H₃O⁺] is greater
H₂ bubbles form faster in the HA beaker, because it contains more acid molecules
No H₂ bubbles form in the HA beaker, because a weak acid does not ionize

questions.stem: Which equation shows the hydrogensulfate ion, HSO₄⁻, acting as a Brønsted–Lowry acid?

options.text: HSO₄⁻ + H₂O ⇌ H₂SO₄ + OH⁻
HSO₄⁻ + H₂O ⇌ SO₄⁻ + H₃O⁺
HSO₄⁻ + H₂O ⇌ SO₄²⁻ + H₃O⁺
HSO₄⁻ + H₃O⁺ ⇌ H₂SO₄ + H₂O

questions.explanation: HSO₄⁻ loses one H⁺ to water, becoming SO₄²⁻. Losing a proton is what an acid does. Charges balance: −1 on each side.

questions.stem: Two solutions are prepared at 25°C: 0.10 M NH₃(aq), a weak base, and 0.10 M NaOH(aq). Which statement correctly compares the solutions?

options.text: [OH⁻] is equal in the two solutions, because each base ionizes completely in water
[OH⁻] is zero in the NH₃ solution, because NH₃ contains no OH group to release
[OH⁻] is lower in the NaOH solution, because NaOH stays mostly as NaOH units
[OH⁻] is lower in the NH₃ solution, because most NH₃ molecules remain un-ionized

questions.explanation: NaOH dissociates completely: [OH⁻] = 0.10 M. Only a small percentage of NH₃ molecules react with water, so [OH⁻] is much less than 0.10 M.

questions.stem: Water takes part in two reactions: (1) CH₃NH₂ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃NH₃⁺ + OH⁻ and (2) HBr + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + Br⁻. What role does water play?

options.text: A base in (1) and an acid in (2)
An acid in both, as it releases H⁺ in each
Neither: it is neutral, so it is only the solvent
An acid in (1) and a base in (2)

questions.explanation: In (1) water donates H⁺ to the N lone pair of CH₃NH₂ and becomes OH⁻. In (2) it accepts H⁺ from HBr and becomes H₃O⁺. Water is amphiprotic: its role depends on its partner.

questions.stem: Methanoic acid is a weak acid: HCOOH(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ HCOO⁻(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq). Which statement is correct?

options.text: The equilibrium lies to the right, as all acids dissociate in water.
The equilibrium lies to the left, as HCOO⁻ is a weaker base than H₂O.
The equilibrium lies to the right, as HCOO⁻ is the weaker of the two bases.
The equilibrium lies to the left, as H₃O⁺ is a stronger acid than HCOOH.

questions.explanation: Equilibrium favours the weaker acid and weaker base. HCOOH is weaker than H₃O⁺, and H₂O weaker than HCOO⁻, so the left is favoured: few molecules dissociate.

questions.stem: Which statement about solutions P and Q is correct? P is 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ M HCl(aq). Q is 0.50 M CH₃COOH(aq), measured pH 2.53.

options.text: P has the lower pH, as a strong acid always has a lower pH than a weak one.
P has the higher pH, even though HCl is the stronger acid.
CH₃COOH must be a strong acid, as Q has a lower pH than P.
HCl is a weak acid in P, as its concentration is low.

questions.explanation: P: pH = −log₁₀(5.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 3.30. Only about 1 in 170 CH₃COOH molecules in Q dissociates, but Q is 1000 times more concentrated, so [H⁺] ≈ 2.95 × 10⁻³, pH 2.53. pH depends on concentration as well as strength.
